claims.title: the **opt-in firewall path** itself (BESS's `firewall`, D-147): the match a PDR compiles to where the WildcardMatch key cannot carry it
claims.declared: **partly in, and unarmed.** `upfd -firewall-ul`/`-firewall-dl` name the module a direction's PDRs go into instead of `-pdr-table-*`: its `<name>/rules` singleton holds the *whole ordered policy*, so the compiler writes every live session's rules of that module (a write of one session's alone would erase the others', and a packet no rule matches is dropped), ordered by Precedence ascending -- 8.2.11's lower value wins and a firewall list applies its first matching rule, so no inversion here -- and replaces it on a deletion and in the startup sweep (an empty policy). A rule's fields are `FirewallArg.Rule`'s: `src_ip`/`dst_ip` (CIDR strings, length mandatory), `proto`, the four port-range bounds, `drop`. What it **cannot** carry is any action: the module's words are drop and pass, it writes no packet metadata, so a rule cannot name the PDR's ActionId or next hop (nor the QFI, the route domain or the tunnel), and a PDR that buffers is refused (no gate to the store). Nothing is live: the installed stage carries no `firewall` module, and a graph that names a module the daemon does not have fails to load, so no `deploy/*.yaml` graph declares one and the arms in `ci/` run the WildcardMatch path with its refusals untouched

claims.title: a restarted controller does not inherit its predecessor's dataplane state: `upfd` empties the session tables in bounded transactions before its PFCP socket opens, and with `-checkpoint` the journal's sessions are replayed after it, so the run holds exactly the sessions it can name
claims.declared: in (docs/design.md's restart wall, no PFCP clause): the sweep reads back one resource per `Contents` call (a call naming several packs them into one response, which the daemon refuses above its 64 MiB message limit: the largest single table is the interim's ceiling -- roughly 510K entries at 131 B each, no paged read, and past it the operator restarts `bessd` -- with its replacement recorded in docs/design.md as a bounded clear in the daemon, which removes the readback), erases exactly the entries it found, key by key, in transactions of a bounded size (at most 1000 changes each, stopping at the first the daemon refuses: a partial sweep is the caller's to refuse) and leaves every resource the graph itself declares; a *firewall policy* has no key to erase -- its resource is a singleton -- so a non-empty one is replaced by an empty policy (a rule's verdict is drop or pass, so one left behind would pass packets no session owns); a dataplane it cannot read back, like a sweep that fails part-way, is fatal at startup rather than served over

claims.title: a restart keeps the sessions rather than losing them, when the run was given a checkpoint

claims.title: **partly fixed**: the **gates** of every QER a PDR names are folded -- a gate closed in any of them stops the rule (resolve), whichever one's rates win. The **GBR** (8.2.7) is the meter's committed rate and the **MBR** (8.2.8) its peak, so the band between them is the meter's yellow gate, wired beside green in every graph (a deployment that marks or sheds that band changes one connection); a GBR above the MBR is refused (cause 73, no meter holds it). The **Averaging Window** (8.2.115, ms) is the meter's burst, where the tree used to write a fixed tenth of a second, and a direction the SMF caps at zero gets no meter rather than a profile the module refuses. **One rule's action carries one meter id** unless the deployment asks for two: then the action names both, the flow's own rate-bearing QER first and the session's shared one after it (below). With one id, a PDR naming several *rate-bearing* QERs is policed by one of them: the session's shared QER -- the most-referenced one, which is how 5.2.1 describes the session's own rate, so the aggregate cap wins rather than whichever QER the SMF listed last -- and a PDR naming only its own flow QER keeps that one. Enforcing every QER's bucket over one packet needs two (or more) meters in the packet's path. **That composition needs no BESS change**: an ActionTable rewrites `meter_id` without consuming the action id, so a second table and a second Meter after the first -- `classifier -> at1 -> m1 -> at2 -> m2` -- give each meter its own id and its own policy, proven on this stage by `ci/meter-compose.sh` (the second meter polices with its own id; had the rewrite not landed it would find no entry and drop fail-closed). Two things that composition needs, both recorded by that lane: every stage's *writes* need a downstream reader or the framework gives them no offset and the module fails closed (`core/metadata.cc`, FillOffsetArrays) -- in the chain the next stage's table, its reader and the Router are those readers -- and the accounting differs from one pass over all buckets: a packet the first meter drops never reaches the second, so the order decides what the aggregate counts: with the flow's meter first, the session's counts only traffic the flow policed through -- the aggregate still caps everything that leaves, and the session can reach its allowance -- while with the session's meter first it also charges packets the flow's meter would have dropped, so the session's own allowance is spent on traffic it never sent (the cap holds either way; which is wanted is the compiler's decision, finding 23) and the two buckets are not updated atomically (finding 23 tracks the compiler work). **The one-action form is now in the fork**: a Meter takes an ordered list of ids (`meter_ids`), checks them in that order, and a packet a level marks red is not charged to the levels after it (BESS fork PR #44); the compiler writes the PDR's own rate-bearing QER first and the session's shared one after it when the direction's level count is 2 (`-meter-levels-ul/-dl`, `ownMeterID`/`sharedMeterID`), so one lookup polices both buckets with the flow's decision final. 0 and 1 are the historical single `meter_id`, which every deployed graph keeps because it declares no `levels`; a graph that does declares `levels: 2` on both its Meter and ActionTable -- the framework refuses a pair that disagrees, the table refuses a longer list -- and the stage this tree runs does not carry the fork change yet. **QER Correlation ID** (8.2.10) is CP-side by construction -- it correlates QERs *across PFCP sessions* -- and leaves a UP with nothing to enforce
